claim: Sex differences in vertebrate spatial abilities are typically interpreted under the adaptive specialization hypothesis, which posits that male reproductive success is linked to larger home ranges and better navigational skills.
source: Sex differences in vertebrate spatial abilities are typically interpreted under the adaptive specialization hypothesis, which posits that male reproductive success is linked to larger home ranges and better navigational skills.
evidence: This is a statement about how sex differences are interpreted in the literature, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The androgen spillover hypothesis counters that enhanced male spatial performance may be a byproduct of higher androgen levels.
source: The androgen spillover hypothesis counters that enhanced male spatial performance may be a byproduct of higher androgen levels.
evidence: This is a statement about an alternative hypothesis, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Contrasting parental sex roles shape sex differences in space use in three species of poison frogs.
source: We tracked individuals in natural environments to show that contrasting parental sex roles shape sex differences in space use, where the sex performing parental duties shows wider-ranging movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by tracking data presented in the results section and Figure 1.

claim: The sex performing parental duties shows wider-ranging movements in poison frogs.
source: We tracked individuals in natural environments to show that contrasting parental sex roles shape sex differences in space use, where the sex performing parental duties shows wider-ranging movements.
evidence: This is supported by tracking data showing movement patterns associated with parental care.

claim: The caring sex outperformed the non-caring sex in navigational performance only in one out of three poison frog species.
source: We then translocated frogs from their home areas to test their navigational performance and found that the caring sex outperformed the non-caring sex only in one out of three species.
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in the results.

claim: Males across poison frog species displayed more explorative behavior than females.
source: In addition, males across species displayed more explorative behavior than females and androgen levels correlated with explorative behavior and homing accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by data from translocation experiments showing explored area measurements.

claim: Androgen levels correlated with explorative behavior in poison frogs.
source: In addition, males across species displayed more explorative behavior than females and androgen levels correlated with explorative behavior and homing accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by hormone measurements and behavioral data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Androgen levels correlated with homing accuracy in poison frogs.
source: In addition, males across species displayed more explorative behavior than females and androgen levels correlated with explorative behavior and homing accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by hormone measurements and navigational performance data.

claim: Poison frog reproductive strategies shape movement patterns but not necessarily navigational performance.
source: Overall, we reveal that poison frog reproductive strategies shape movement patterns but not necessarily navigational performance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined results of space use and navigation experiments.

claim: Prevailing adaptive hypotheses provide an incomplete explanation of sex differences in spatial abilities.
source: Together this work suggests that prevailing adaptive hypotheses provide an incomplete explanation of sex differences in spatial abilities.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the study's findings not fully supporting the adaptive specialization hypothesis.

claim: In mammals, males tend to have larger home ranges and enhanced navigational skill compared to females.
source: Sex differences in spatial abilities are well established in mammals, where males tend to have larger home ranges and enhanced navigational skill compared to females (Clint et al., 2012; Gray and Buffery, 1971; Jonasson, 2005; Jones et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In rodents, sex differences in space use have been linked to reproductive strategy, where polygamous species show sex differences in home range size and spatial abilities, but monogamous species do not.
source: In a series of comparative rodent studies, sex differences in space use have been linked to reproductive strategy, where polygamous species show sex differences in home range size and spatial abilities, but monogamous species do not (Galea et al., 1994; Gaulin et al., 1990; Gaulin and FitzGerald, 1986; Gaulin and Fitzgerald, 1989; Sawrey et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative rodent studies.

claim: In humans, men tend to score higher on spatial tests related to 3D mental rotations.
source: In humans, men tend to score higher on spatial tests related to 3D mental rotations, whereas women tend to score better on object location memory (Eals and Silverman, 1994; Silverman et al., 2007; Voyer et al., 1995; reviewed in Clint et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human spatial cognition studies.

claim: In humans, women tend to score better on object location memory.
source: In humans, men tend to score higher on spatial tests related to 3D mental rotations, whereas women tend to score better on object location memory (Eals and Silverman, 1994; Silverman et al., 2007; Voyer et al., 1995; reviewed in Clint et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human spatial cognition studies.

claim: Maternal care in mammals may limit space use and exploration in females.
source: In addition, maternal care in mammals may limit space use and exploration in females (Barnett and McEwan, 1973; Sherry and Hampson, 1997; Trivers, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Empirical support for the adaptive specialization hypothesis outside rodents is often inconclusive.
source: While the adaptive specialization hypothesis has been widely accepted for decades, empirical support outside rodents is often inconclusive and alternative explanations are rarely evaluated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, based on review of existing studies.

claim: Human sex differences in spatial abilities are not universal, but are influenced by cultural and population-specific factors such as mobility related to lifestyle.
source: Cross-cultural studies show that human sex differences in spatial abilities are not universal, but are influenced by cultural and population-specific factors such as mobility related to lifestyle (Berry, 1966; Cashdan et al., 2012; Jang et al., 2019; Trumble et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cross-cultural studies.

claim: Higher androgen levels in mammals enhance spatial performance through effects on neural development and plasticity.
source: Higher androgen levels in mammals enhance spatial performance through effects on neural development and plasticity (Dawson et al., 1975; Galea et al., 1995; Isgor and Sengelaub, 1998; Joseph et al., 1978; Neave et al., 1999; Roof and Havens, 1992; Schulz and Korz, 2010; Sherry and Hampson, 1997; Stewart et al., 1975; Van Goozen et al., 1995; Williams et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience studies.

claim: In humans, female performance in spatial ability tasks correlates positively with androgen levels and improves with androgen treatments.
source: In humans, female performance in spatial ability tasks correlates positively with androgen levels and improves with androgen treatments (Aleman et al., 2004; Burkitt et al., 2007; Driscoll et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human hormone studies.

claim: In brood-parasitic cowbirds, females have larger forebrain areas associated with spatial learning in comparison to males and non-parasitic relatives.
source: In brood-parasitic cowbirds, where females need to remember and locate multiple host nest sites, females have larger forebrain areas associated with spatial learning in comparison to males and non-parasitic relatives (Sherry et al., 1993; Reboreda et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cowbird neuroanatomy studies.

claim: The outcomes of behavioral studies of sex difference in cowbirds' spatial abilities are inconclusive.
source: However, the outcomes of behavioral studies of sex difference in cowbirds' spatial abilities are inconclusive as some (Guigueno et al., 2014), but not others (Astié et al., 1998; Astié et al., 2015; Lois-Milevicich et al., 2021), found the expected female advantage in spatial tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies in cowbirds.

claim: In Blenniid fishes, males defend small territories and perform parental care while females move between males and have larger home ranges.
source: In Blenniid fishes males defend small territories and perform parental care while females move between males, and have larger home ranges and larger forebrain areas associated with spatial cognition than males (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Blenniid fishes.

claim: Blenniid fish females have larger forebrain areas associated with spatial cognition than males.
source: In Blenniid fishes males defend small territories and perform parental care while females move between males, and have larger home ranges and larger forebrain areas associated with spatial cognition than males (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Blenniid fishes.

claim: Behavioral testing in one blenny species and some other fishes found fewer or opposite sex differences than predicted by the adaptive specialization hypothesis.
source: However, behavioral testing in one blenny species (Fabre et al., 2014) and some other fishes (Keagy et al., 2019; Wallace and Hofmann, 2021) found fewer or opposite sex differences than predicted by the adaptive specialization hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies in fishes.

claim: Amphibians show a remarkable variety of mating strategies and parental sex roles compared to mammals and birds, including widespread polyandry and male uniparental care.
source: Amphibians show a remarkable variety of mating strategies and parental sex roles compared to mammals and birds, including widespread polyandry and male uniparental care (Duellman, 1989; Schulte et al., 2020; Wells, 1977; Zamudio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to amphibian behavioral ecology literature.

claim: In Neotropical poison frogs, male and female uniparental care, biparental care, and flexible parental roles occur among closely related species.
source: In Neotropical poison frogs (Dendrobatoidea), male and female uniparental care, biparental care, and flexible parental roles occur among closely related species (Schulte et al., 2020; Summers and Tumulty, 2014; Weygoldt, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to poison frog literature.

claim: Poison frog parental care involves complex spatial behavior, where parents navigate the rainforest to transport tadpoles from terrestrial clutches to pools of water.
source: Poison frog parental care involves complex spatial behavior, where parents navigate the rainforest to transport tadpoles from terrestrial clutches to pools of water (Beck et al., 2017; Pašukonis et al., 2019; Ringler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous poison frog studies.

claim: Poison frogs show well-developed spatial cognition and rely on spatial memory to relocate home territories and tadpole deposition sites.
source: Poison frogs show well-developed spatial cognition and rely on spatial memory to relocate home territories and tadpole deposition sites (Beck et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2016; Stynoski, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous poison frog cognition studies.

claim: Male tadpole transport is the ancestral and most common form of parental care in poison frogs.
source: Male tadpole transport is the ancestral and most common form of parental care in poison frogs (Carvajal-Castro et al., 2021; Summers and Tumulty, 2014; Weygoldt, 1987), but female care and flexible parental roles have evolved in some species (Fischer and O'Connell, 2020; Ringler et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to poison frog evolutionary and behavioral studies.

claim: Female care and flexible parental roles have evolved in some poison frog species.
source: Male tadpole transport is the ancestral and most common form of parental care in poison frogs (Carvajal-Castro et al., 2021; Summers and Tumulty, 2014; Weygoldt, 1987), but female care and flexible parental roles have evolved in some species (Fischer and O'Connell, 2020; Ringler et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to poison frog studies.

claim: In poison frog species where females provide care, frogs place their tadpoles in small, resource-poor nurseries and females frequently return to these pools to supplement the tadpoles' diet by provisioning with unfertilized eggs.
source: In species where females provide care, frogs place their tadpoles in small, resource-poor nurseries. Females frequently return to these pools to supplement the tadpoles' diet by provisioning with unfertilized eggs (Brust, 1990; Summers and Tumulty, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to poison frog parental care studies.

claim: Poison frogs show sex-typical differences in androgen levels, where males have higher androgen levels than females.
source: Poison frogs also show sex-typical differences in androgen levels, where males have higher androgen levels than females, although androgen levels decrease during tadpole transport in males (Fischer and O'Connell, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Androgen levels decrease during tadpole transport in male poison frogs.
source: Poison frogs also show sex-typical differences in androgen levels, where males have higher androgen levels than females, although androgen levels decrease during tadpole transport in males (Fischer and O'Connell, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In A. femoralis, the average male home range was 153% larger than females.
source: In A. femoralis, where males do most parental care duties, the average male home range was 153% larger and movement extent 172% larger than females (Figure 1, Table 1, Supplementary file 1, Table 1a).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: In A. femoralis, male movement extent was 172% larger than females.
source: In A. femoralis, where males do most parental care duties, the average male home range was 153% larger and movement extent 172% larger than females (Figure 1, Table 1, Supplementary file 1, Table 1a).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Long-term movements based on capture–recapture data were larger in males than in females of A. femoralis.
source: We also found that long-term movements based on capture–recapture data were larger in males than in females of A. femoralis (LM: βextent male = 0.55, t = 3.1, n = 165, p = 0.002; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by capture-recapture data analysis presented in the results.

claim: In D. tinctorius, there was no significant sex difference in home range size or movement extent based on tracking data.
source: In D. tinctorius, where males perform parental care, we found no significant sex differences in home range size or movement extent based on tracking data, but males showed wider-ranging long-term movements based on capture–recapture data (LM: βextent male = 0.43, t = 2.62, n = 154, p = 0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data analysis presented in the results.

claim: In D. tinctorius, males showed wider-ranging long-term movements based on capture–recapture data.
source: In D. tinctorius, where males perform parental care, we found no significant sex differences in home range size or movement extent based on tracking data, but males showed wider-ranging long-term movements based on capture–recapture data (LM: βextent male = 0.43, t = 2.62, n = 154, p = 0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by capture-recapture data analysis.

claim: In O. sylvatica, the average male home range was 56% smaller than in females.
source: In O. sylvatica, where females perform parental care, the average male home range was 56% smaller and movement extent 57% smaller than in females.
evidence: This is supported by tracking data presented in the results.

claim: In O. sylvatica, male movement extent was 57% smaller than in females.
source: In O. sylvatica, where females perform parental care, the average male home range was 56% smaller and movement extent 57% smaller than in females.
evidence: This is supported by tracking data presented in the results.

claim: There was no sex difference in O. sylvatica daily travel at the natural site.
source: There was no sex difference in the O. sylvatica daily travel at the natural site (LMM: βdaily male = −0.27, t = −1.6, n = 93, p = 0.1) nor within enclosures (LMM: βdaily male = −0.11, t = –1, n = 287, p = 0.3), but short-term movement extent was larger in females than in males of O. sylvatica at both the natural site (LM: βextent male = −0.38, t = −2.4, n = 37, p = 0.02) and within enclosures (LM: βextent male = −0.42, t = −2.9, n = 29, p = 0.007; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of tracking data.

claim: Short-term movement extent was larger in females than in males of O. sylvatica at both the natural site and within enclosures.
source: There was no sex difference in the O. sylvatica daily travel at the natural site (LMM: βdaily male = −0.27, t = −1.6, n = 93, p = 0.1) nor within enclosures (LMM: βdaily male = −0.11, t = –1, n = 287, p = 0.3), but short-term movement extent was larger in females than in males of O. sylvatica at both the natural site (LM: βextent male = −0.38, t = −2.4, n = 37, p = 0.02) and within enclosures (LM: βextent male = −0.42, t = −2.9, n = 29, p = 0.007; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of tracking data.

claim: A. femoralis males moved more on days of parental care than on mating days and other days.
source: A. femoralis males moved more on days of parental care than on mating days (lsm contrast: β = 1.8, p < 0.001) and other days (lsm contrast: β = 1.9, p < 0.001), but equally between mating days and other days (lsm contrast p = 0.75; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: A. femoralis females moved more on days of mating than other days.
source: A. femoralis females moved more on days of mating than other days (lsm contrast: β = 0.6, p < 0.001) and were only observed transporting tadpoles once (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: A. femoralis females were only observed transporting tadpoles once.
source: A. femoralis females moved more on days of mating than other days (lsm contrast: β = 0.6, p < 0.001) and were only observed transporting tadpoles once (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracking study.

claim: D. tinctorius males moved more on days of parental care than on mating days and other days.
source: D. tinctorius males also moved more on days of parental care than on mating days (lsm contrast: β = 1.3, p < 0.001) and other days (lsm contrast: β = 1.5, p < 0.001), but moved equally between mating days and other days (lsm contrast p = 0.85, Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: Daily travel of D. tinctorius females did not differ on days of mating from other days.
source: Daily travel of D. tinctorius females did not differ on days of mating from other days (lsm contrast p = 0.4, Figure 1), and females were never observed in the pools or with tadpoles.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: D. tinctorius females were never observed in the pools or with tadpoles.
source: Daily travel of D. tinctorius females did not differ on days of mating from other days (lsm contrast p = 0.4, Figure 1), and females were never observed in the pools or with tadpoles.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracking study.

claim: Daily travel of O. sylvatica males did not differ between mating days and other days.
source: Daily travel of O. sylvatica males did not differ between mating days and other days (lsm contrast p = 0.95, Figure 1) and males were never seen transporting tadpoles, but were regularly found near the breeding pools often located inside their territories.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: O. sylvatica males were never seen transporting tadpoles.
source: Daily travel of O. sylvatica males did not differ between mating days and other days (lsm contrast p = 0.95, Figure 1) and males were never seen transporting tadpoles, but were regularly found near the breeding pools often located inside their territories.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracking study.

claim: O. sylvatica males were regularly found near the breeding pools often located inside their territories.
source: Daily travel of O. sylvatica males did not differ between mating days and other days (lsm contrast p = 0.95, Figure 1) and males were never seen transporting tadpoles, but were regularly found near the breeding pools often located inside their territories.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracking study.

claim: O. sylvatica females moved more on days of parental care than on other days.
source: Females of O. sylvatica moved more on days of parental care than on other days (lsm contrast: β = 0.4, p = 0.004; Figure 1), but there was no difference between mating days and parental days (lsm contrast p = 0.8) or other days (lsm contrast p = 0.3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of daily travel data.

claim: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males were more likely to return home (81% males, 44% females).
source: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males were more likely to return home (81% males, 44% females), but both sexes of D. tinctorius (94% males, 94% females) and O. sylvatica (80% males vs. 70% females) were equally likely to return (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: When translocated 50 m, both sexes of D. tinctorius (94% males, 94% females) were equally likely to return home.
source: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males were more likely to return home (81% males, 44% females), but both sexes of D. tinctorius (94% males, 94% females) and O. sylvatica (80% males vs. 70% females) were equally likely to return (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: When translocated 50 m, both sexes of O. sylvatica (80% males vs. 70% females) were equally likely to return home.
source: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males were more likely to return home (81% males, 44% females), but both sexes of D. tinctorius (94% males, 94% females) and O. sylvatica (80% males vs. 70% females) were equally likely to return (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: When translocated 200 m, only males of A. femoralis (75% males, 0% females) were able to return home.
source: When translocated 200 m, only males of A. femoralis (75% males, 0% females) and both females and males of D. tinctorius (56% males, 39% females), but no O. sylvatica were able to return home (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: When translocated 200 m, both females and males of D. tinctorius (56% males, 39% females) were able to return home.
source: When translocated 200 m, only males of A. femoralis (75% males, 0% females) and both females and males of D. tinctorius (56% males, 39% females), but no O. sylvatica were able to return home (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: When translocated 200 m, no O. sylvatica were able to return home.
source: When translocated 200 m, only males of A. femoralis (75% males, 0% females) and both females and males of D. tinctorius (56% males, 39% females), but no O. sylvatica were able to return home (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by translocation experiment data presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: A. femoralis were less likely to return home with higher daytime temperature.
source: A. femoralis were less likely to return home with higher daytime temperature, but the daytime temperature had no effect on homing success in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: Daytime temperature had no effect on homing success in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica.
source: A. femoralis were less likely to return home with higher daytime temperature, but the daytime temperature had no effect on homing success in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: Frog weight had no effect on homing success.
source: Frog weight had no effect on homing success.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males explored larger areas than females.
source: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males explored larger areas than females, but we observed no sex difference in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: When translocated 50 m, there was no sex difference in explored area in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica.
source: When translocated 50 m, A. femoralis males explored larger areas than females, but we observed no sex difference in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: When translocated 200 m, males of all three species were more explorative than females.
source: When translocated 200 m, males of all three species were more explorative than females (Figure 3 and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: A. femoralis explored less with higher daytime temperature.
source: In addition, A. femoralis explored less with higher daytime temperature, but the daytime temperature did not affect the explored area in D. tinctorius or O. sylvatica (Table 3, Supplementary file 1, Table 1b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Daytime temperature did not affect the explored area in D. tinctorius or O. sylvatica.
source: In addition, A. femoralis explored less with higher daytime temperature, but the daytime temperature did not affect the explored area in D. tinctorius or O. sylvatica (Table 3, Supplementary file 1, Table 1b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Frog weight positively influenced the explored area only in D. tinctorius translocated 200 m.
source: Frog weight positively influenced the explored area only in D. tinctorius translocated 200 m (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: After 50-m translocation, A. femoralis males returned more directly and faster than females.
source: After 50-m translocation, A. femoralis males returned more directly and faster than females (Figure 3, Table 4 and Supplementary file 1, Table 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: After moving ~20% of the translocation distance from the release site, A. femoralis males but not females were significantly oriented toward home.
source: After moving ~20% of the translocation distance from the release site, A. femoralis males but not females were significantly oriented toward home (50 m: male Rayleigh p < 0.001, female Rayleigh p = 0.15; 200 m: male Rayleigh p < 0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by circular statistics presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a sex difference in the distribution of angular deviations in A. femoralis.
source: We also found a sex difference in the distribution of angular deviations in A. femoralis (F(22) = 3.9, p = 0.03).
evidence: This is supported by MANOVA analysis.

claim: In D. tinctorius, females returned in more direct paths than males from 200 m.
source: In D. tinctorius, females returned in more direct paths than males from 200 m (Figure 3 and Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: Both males and females of D. tinctorius were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m.
source: Both males and females of D. tinctorius were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.007, female Rayleigh p < 0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but not when translocated 200 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.4, female Rayleigh p = 0.85; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by circular statistics presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: D. tinctorius males and females were not significantly oriented when translocated 200 m.
source: Both males and females of D. tinctorius were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.007, female Rayleigh p < 0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but not when translocated 200 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.4, female Rayleigh p = 0.85; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by circular statistics presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no sex differences in the distribution of angular deviations in D. tinctorius.
source: There were no sex differences in the distribution of angular deviations in D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on MANOVA analysis.

claim: In O. sylvatica, there was no sex difference in trajectory straightness, homing duration, or the distribution of angular deviations.
source: In O. sylvatica, we found no sex difference in trajectory straightness, homing duration, or the distribution of angular deviations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: After moving ~20% of the translocation distance, males but not females of O. sylvatica were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m.
source: After moving ~20% of the translocation distance, males but not females of O. sylvatica were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.015, female Rayleigh p = 0.18; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but not after 200 m translocation (male Rayleigh p = 0.9, female Rayleigh p = 0.9; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by circular statistics presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: O. sylvatica males and females were not significantly oriented after 200 m translocation.
source: After moving ~20% of the translocation distance, males but not females of O. sylvatica were significantly oriented when translocated 50 m (male Rayleigh p = 0.015, female Rayleigh p = 0.18; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but not after 200 m translocation (male Rayleigh p = 0.9, female Rayleigh p = 0.9; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by circular statistics presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A. femoralis and O. sylvatica returned in less direct paths and slower with higher daytime temperature.
source: A. femoralis and O. sylvatica returned in less direct paths and slower with higher daytime temperature.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: D. tinctorius returned slower with higher daytime temperature, but temperature had no effect on trajectory straightness.
source: Dendrobates tinctorius returned slower with higher daytime temperature, but temperature had no effect on trajectory straightness (Table 4, Supplementary file 1, Table 1c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Frog weight did not affect the homing duration.
source: Frog weight did not affect the homing duration.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: Males showed higher androgen levels in all three poison frog species.
source: There was high interindividual variation of androgen levels in both sexes of all species, but on average, males showed higher androgen levels in all three species (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1d).
evidence: This is supported by hormone measurement data presented in Figure 4.

claim: There were no significant differences between baseline and back-home androgen samples in all three species.
source: There were no significant differences between baseline and back-home samples in all three species.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: Baseline androgen levels did not influence exploration, homing duration, nor trajectory straightness in A. femoralis.
source: Baseline levels did not influence exploration, homing duration, nor trajectory straightness in A. femoralis (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1e).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Baseline androgen levels, together with sex, translocation distance, and frog weight significantly predicted exploration in D. tinctorius.
source: Baseline androgen levels, together with sex, translocation distance, and frog weight significantly predicted exploration in D. tinctorius, but did not influence homing duration or trajectory straightness (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1f).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Baseline androgen levels did not influence homing duration or trajectory straightness in D. tinctorius.
source: Baseline androgen levels, together with sex, translocation distance, and frog weight significantly predicted exploration in D. tinctorius, but did not influence homing duration or trajectory straightness (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1A, Table 1f).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Baseline androgen levels significantly predicted trajectory straightness in O. sylvatica.
source: Baseline levels significantly predicted trajectory straightness, but not exploration or homing duration in O. sylvatica (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1, Table 1g).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Baseline androgen levels did not predict exploration or homing duration in O. sylvatica.
source: Baseline levels significantly predicted trajectory straightness, but not exploration or homing duration in O. sylvatica (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1, Table 1g).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The explored area had a significant positive effect on delta androgen levels in A. femoralis.
source: The explored area had a significant positive effect and successful homing a significant negative effect on delta androgen levels in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Supplementary file 1, Table 1h).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Successful homing had a significant negative effect on delta androgen levels in A. femoralis.
source: The explored area had a significant positive effect and successful homing a significant negative effect on delta androgen levels in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Supplementary file 1, Table 1h).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Explored area and successful homing did not affect delta androgen levels in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica.
source: The explored area had a significant positive effect and successful homing a significant negative effect on delta androgen levels in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica (Supplementary file 1, Table 1h).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: All three poison frog species showed well-developed homing ability.
source: All three species showed well-developed homing ability, which is consistent with previous studies in amphibians, including various anurans (Arcila-Pérez et al., 2020; Dole, 1968; McVey et al., 1981; Navarro-Salcedo et al., 2021; Navarro-Salcedo et al., 2022; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2018; Pichler et al., 2017; Shaykevich et al., 2021; Sinsch, 1987; Sinsch, 1992) and caudates (Diego-Rasilla et al., 2005; Grant et al., 1968; Joly and Miaud, 1989; Phillips et al., 1995; Sinsch, 2007; Twitty et al., 1964; reviewed in Ferguson, 1971; Sinsch, 2006; Wells, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous amphibian studies.

claim: O. sylvatica did not return from longer translocation distances, in line with their much smaller home ranges relative to A. femoralis and D. tinctorius.
source: For example, O. sylvatica did not return from longer translocation distances, in line with their much smaller home ranges relative to A. femoralis and D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between home range size and homing performance observed in the data.

claim: The correlation between home range size and homing performance supports the hypothesis that poison frogs rely on exploration and spatial learning for navigation.
source: This apparent correlation between home range size and homing performance further supports the hypothesis that poison frogs rely on exploration and spatial learning for navigation (Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2016; Pašukonis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation and citations to previous studies.

claim: The distances from which poison frogs navigate back home exceed the extent of observed routine movements.
source: Surprisingly, the distances from which poison frogs navigate back home exceed the extent of observed routine movements (Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2018; this study) leaving many open questions about the possible cues learned and used for orientation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of homing distances and home range data from this study and previous studies.

claim: After translocation, A. femoralis tended to stay close to the release site for prolonged periods and then navigate back home via a direct path.
source: After translocation, A. femoralis tended to stay close to the release site for prolonged periods and then navigate back home via a direct path.
evidence: This is a description of movement patterns observed in the tracking data.

claim: Non-homing A. femoralis individuals moved very little and remained close to the release site.
source: Non-homing individuals moved very little and remained close to the release site.
evidence: This is a description of movement patterns observed in the tracking data.

claim: D. tinctorius showed wide-ranging exploratory movements and usually returned home through an indirect and lengthy route.
source: However, D. tinctorius showed wide-ranging exploratory movements and usually returned home through an indirect and lengthy route.
evidence: This is a description of movement patterns observed in the tracking data.

claim: O. sylvatica showed some wide-ranging exploratory behavior that was never observed in A. femoralis.
source: Similarly, even though O. sylvatica returned home only from shorter distances, they also showed some wide-ranging exploratory behavior that was never observed in A. femoralis.
evidence: This is a description of movement patterns observed in the tracking data.

claim: D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica are brightly colored species that forage actively to acquire their alkaloid-based chemical defenses from the invertebrate diet.
source: D. tinctorius and O. sylvatica are brightly colored species that forage actively to acquire their alkaloid-based chemical defenses from the invertebrate diet (Santos et al., 2016; Santos and Cannatella, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on poison frog chemical ecology.

claim: Aposematic coloration may reduce predation pressure and the cost of movement while potentially increasing exploration.
source: Aposematic coloration may reduce predation pressure and the cost of movement while potentially increasing exploration (Carvajal-Castro et al., 2021; Pough and Taigen, 1990; Speed et al., 2010; Summers, 2019; Toft, 1981), allowing different navigational strategies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A. femoralis is cryptically colored, non-toxic, and a generalist sit-and-wait forager.
source: A. femoralis, on the other hand, is cryptically colored, non-toxic, and a generalist sit-and-wait forager.
evidence: This is a description of the species' natural history based on established knowledge.

claim: The only two predation events observed during tracking occurred in A. femoralis.
source: The only two predation events observed during tracking occurred in A. femoralis and we have regularly observed predation and predation-related injuries during the long-term capture–recapture monitoring in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the field study.

claim: Predation and predation-related injuries have been regularly observed during long-term capture–recapture monitoring in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius.
source: The only two predation events observed during tracking occurred in A. femoralis and we have regularly observed predation and predation-related injuries during the long-term capture–recapture monitoring in A. femoralis, but not in D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the field study.

claim: Predation pressure is likely to be much higher and the movement more costly for cryptic species, potentially selecting more efficient orientation strategies.
source: Thus, the predation pressure is likely to be much higher and the movement more costly for cryptic species, potentially selecting more efficient orientation strategies.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed predation patterns and species differences in coloration.

claim: There was no sex difference in the navigational performance of D. tinctorius.
source: Contrary to our prediction, we found no sex difference in the navigational performance of D. tinctorius, a species with male uniparental care.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: D. tinctorius females showed slightly more accurate homing trajectories than males when navigating long distances.
source: Not only did males not outperform females, but females even showed slightly more accurate homing trajectories than males when navigating long distances.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: There were no sex differences in the navigational performance of O. sylvatica.
source: Crucially, although females of O. sylvatica have larger space use and perform tadpole transport and egg provisioning, we found no sex differences in the navigational performance.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: Place discrimination tasks have not revealed consistent sex differences in Engystomops pustulosus.
source: Place discrimination tasks have not revealed consistent sex differences in Engystomops pustulusos, a frog species where females seek for and move between males (Liu and Burmeister, 2017; Ventura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A recent study in Andinobates bombetes found no sex differences in homing rates after translocation.
source: Using translocation and recapture methods, one recent study in Andinobates bombetes, a poison frog with male uniparental care, found no sex differences in homing rates after translocation (Arcila-Pérez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A recent recapture study in the glass frog Ikakogi tayrona found that only males, but not females, showed homing after translocations.
source: Another recent recapture study in the glass frog Ikakogi tayrona, a species with prolonged maternal care and male territoriality, found that only males, but not females, showed homing after translocations (Navarro-Salcedo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A. femoralis males were more likely to return home, returned from longer distances, and returned faster and more accurately than females.
source: The only species with marked sex differences in navigational performance was A. femoralis, where males were more likely to return home, returned from longer distances, and returned faster and more accurately than females.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: A. femoralis females commute between males for reproduction.
source: This finding is partially unexpected because A. femoralis females commute between males for reproduction (Fischer et al., 2020; Ringler et al., 2012) and remember the exact locations of their clutches (Ringler et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A. femoralis females remember the exact locations of their clutches.
source: This finding is partially unexpected because A. femoralis females commute between males for reproduction (Fischer et al., 2020; Ringler et al., 2012) and remember the exact locations of their clutches (Ringler et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Non-homing A. femoralis females typically stay stationary.
source: As non-homing A. femoralis females typically stay stationary, it is difficult to disentangle the lack of motivation from their inability to return home.
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior in the navigation experiments.

claim: A. femoralis females show site fidelity.
source: We expected that A. femoralis females would be motivated to return home because they show site fidelity (Fischer et al., 2020; Ringler et al., 2009; this study) and monitor the presence of their mating partners to eventually take over tadpole transport in case of male absence (Ringler et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from this study.

claim: A. femoralis females monitor the presence of their mating partners to eventually take over tadpole transport in case of male absence.
source: We expected that A. femoralis females would be motivated to return home because they show site fidelity (Fischer et al., 2020; Ringler et al., 2009; this study) and monitor the presence of their mating partners to eventually take over tadpole transport in case of male absence (Ringler et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A. femoralis females returned, albeit slower from shorter translocation distances, indicating that they were motivated to return in a sufficiently familiar area.
source: Indeed, females returned, albeit slower from shorter translocation distances, indicating that they were motivated to return in a sufficiently familiar area.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed homing behavior.

claim: Homing A. femoralis females showed less directed homing, suggesting a sex difference in orientation accuracy.
source: In addition, homing females showed less directed homing, suggesting a sex difference in orientation accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed trajectory data.

claim: A. femoralis males may be more motivated to return home quickly because they risk losing both their territory and all current offspring due to territorial takeovers and potential cannibalism by other males.
source: However, males may be more motivated to return home quickly because they risk losing both their territory and all current offspring due to territorial takeovers and potential cannibalism by other males (Ringler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Sex differences in navigational performance were found only in the non-toxic A. femoralis, which likely faces much higher predation pressure than the two aposematic species.
source: Interestingly, we found sex differences only in the non-toxic A. femoralis, which likely faces much higher predation pressure than the two aposematic species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of sex differences and species differences in coloration and predation.

claim: Adaptive sex differences in navigational ability may emerge only under strong predation pressure.
source: It is possible that adaptive sex differences in navigational ability emerge only under strong predation pressure, explaining the lack of selective pressure and sex difference in aposematic O. sylvatica and D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed patterns.

claim: Poison frogs rely on learning for spatial orientation.
source: While there is clear evidence that poison frogs rely on learning for spatial orientation (Beck et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2016; Pašukonis et al., 2019), the exact cognitive mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The exact cognitive mechanisms of poison frog spatial orientation remain unknown.
source: While there is clear evidence that poison frogs rely on learning for spatial orientation (Beck et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2016; Pašukonis et al., 2019), the exact cognitive mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Smaller scale spatial tasks specifically testing for place learning and recall might reveal sex differences in specific spatiocognitive abilities.
source: It is possible that smaller scale spatial tasks specifically testing for place learning and recall (e.g., Liu et al., 2019) would reveal sex differences in specific spatiocognitive abilities, which is particularly relevant for locating clutches and breeding pool in poison frogs (Beck et al., 2017; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Ringler et al., 2016a; Stynoski, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In human studies, naturalistic navigation tasks reveal fewer sex differences than tasks testing specific spatiocognitive ability.
source: In human studies, naturalistic navigation tasks, such as pointing to a distant location, reveal fewer sex differences (Cashdan et al., 2012; Jang et al., 2019; Trumble et al., 2016) than tasks testing specific spatiocognitive ability, such as three-dimensional rotation or object location memory (Silverman et al., 2007; Voyer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human cognition studies.

claim: Sex differences in spatial abilities are task specific in cowbirds and cichlid fish.
source: Sex differences are also task specific in cowbirds (Astié et al., 1998; Astié et al., 2015; Lois-Milevicich et al., 2021) and cichlid fish (Wallace and Hofmann, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Males are bolder and more explorative in several species and taxa.
source: Males are bolder and more explorative in several species and taxa (e.g., fish: Harris et al., 2010; King et al., 2013; bird: Schuett and Dall, 2009) and multiple adaptive hypotheses have been proposed to explain increased exploration (reviewed in Schuett et al., 2010; Trivers, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Male-biased dispersal is common in polygamous mammals while female-biased dispersal is common in monogamous birds.
source: Sex differences in exploration tendency could be connected to the sex-biased dispersal observed in different mating strategies, where male-biased dispersal is common in polygamous mammals while female-biased dispersal is common in monogamous birds (Greenwood, 1980; Li and Kokko, 2019; Mabry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Males of all three poison frog species tended to be more explorative than females, particularly when translocated longer distances.
source: In the present study, males of all three species tended to be more explorative than females, particularly when translocated longer distances and, therefore, in less familiar environments.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: In O. sylvatica, males tended to be more explorative after translocations even though females perform parental care and have wider space use.
source: Even in O. sylvatica, a species where females perform parental care and have wider space use, males tended to be more explorative after translocations.
evidence: This is supported by the navigation experiment data.

claim: Male-biased dispersal and higher male exploration rates have been observed in some frogs without parental care.
source: Male-biased dispersal and higher male exploration rates have also been observed in some frogs without parental care (Engystomops pustulosus: Lampert et al., 2003; Bufo bufo: Ogurtsov et al., 2018; Xenopus tropicalis: Videlier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regardless of parental care strategies, different life histories, and sex differences in home range size, male amphibians tend to be more exploratory.
source: Thus, regardless of parental care strategies, different life histories, and sex differences in home range size, male amphibians tend to be more exploratory, suggesting that other factors, such as male-biased dispersal and high intrasexual male competition may be associated with the sex difference in exploration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern across species and citations to previous studies.

claim: Androgens have been linked to spatial abilities in mammals for several decades.
source: Androgens have been linked to spatial abilities in mammals for several decades (Dawson et al., 1975; Galea et al., 1995; Isgor and Sengelaub, 1998; Joseph et al., 1978; Schulz and Korz, 2010; Sherry and Hampson, 1997; Stewart et al., 1975; Williams et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Higher baseline androgen levels predicted more exploration after translocation in D. tinctorius.
source: Higher baseline androgen levels predicted more exploration after translocation in D. tinctorius, and the amount of exploration during the navigation task was associated with an increase in androgen levels in A. femoralis.
evidence: This is supported by hormone and behavioral data analysis.

claim: The amount of exploration during the navigation task was associated with an increase in androgen levels in A. femoralis.
source: Higher baseline androgen levels predicted more exploration after translocation in D. tinctorius, and the amount of exploration during the navigation task was associated with an increase in androgen levels in A. femoralis.
evidence: This is supported by hormone and behavioral data analysis.

claim: Males had higher androgen levels and higher exploration rates despite the variation in the parental sex roles and high interindividual variation.
source: We also found that males, on average, had higher androgen levels and higher exploration rates despite the variation in the parental sex roles and high interindividual variation.
evidence: This is supported by hormone and behavioral data.

claim: Exploration underlies the development of most spatiocognitive abilities.
source: Exploration underlies the development of most spatiocognitive abilities (McNaughton et al., 2006; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978), including spatial memory, presumably used by poison frogs for navigation (Beck et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Pašukonis et al., 2014; Pašukonis et al., 2016; Pašukonis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cognitive neuroscience and poison frog studies.

claim: The association of explorative behavior with androgen levels, especially during the development of spatial memory, might have cascading effects on sex differences in spatial behavior and abilities.
source: Therefore, the association of explorative behavior with androgen levels, especially during the development of spatial memory, might have cascading effects on sex differences in spatial behavior and abilities.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed associations and knowledge of cognitive development.

claim: Baseline androgens correlated with homing accuracy in O. sylvatica in both sexes.
source: We also found that baseline androgens correlated with homing accuracy in O. sylvatica in both sexes, further supporting a potential link between androgens and navigational performance.
evidence: This is supported by hormone and behavioral data analysis.

claim: Parental behavior drives space use patterns in poison frogs.
source: We found that parental behavior drives space use patterns but not navigational performance in poison frogs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined results.

claim: Most observed sex differences indicated more developed navigational ability and increased exploratory tendency in males, even in species where females show wider-ranging movement for parental care and mate-seeking.
source: Most observed sex differences indicated more developed navigational ability and increased exploratory tendency in males, even in species where females show wider-ranging movement for parental care and mate-seeking.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Most previous literature on sex differences in vertebrate spatial abilities shows either no sex differences or better performance in males.
source: Indeed, most previous literature on sex differences in vertebrate spatial abilities shows either no sex differences or better performance in males.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on review.

claim: There was a high interindividual variation in androgens and a large overlap between sexes in all three poison frog species.
source: We also found higher average androgen levels in males of all three species despite the marked species differences in parental sex roles and aggressive female behavior. However, there was a high interindividual variation in androgens and a large overlap between sexes.
evidence: This is supported by hormone measurement data.

claim: Some of the interindividual variation in androgen levels was related to individual differences in exploration and homing accuracy.
source: Some of this interindividual variation in androgen levels was related to individual differences in exploration and homing accuracy, suggesting an interplay between androgens and spatial behavior.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of hormone and behavioral data.

claim: The findings are more consistent with the androgen spillover hypothesis than the adaptive specialization hypothesis.
source: Therefore, our findings are more consistent with the androgen spillover hypothesis than the widely accepted adaptive specialization hypothesis based on sex difference in home range size or the complexity of spatial behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the pattern of results.

claim: Sex differences in spatial abilities could be a byproduct of selective pressures on sexual traits such as aggressiveness and the associated increase in androgen levels.
source: We speculate that sex differences in spatial abilities could be a byproduct of selective pressures on sexual traits such as aggressiveness and the associated increase in androgen levels.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed patterns.

claim: The indirect effects of androgens, such as increased male exploration tendency, are likely to be adaptive and maintained in the context of male territoriality and widespread male parental care in poison frogs.
source: However, the indirect effects of androgens, such as increased male exploration tendency, are likely to be adaptive and maintained in the context of male territoriality and widespread male parental care in poison frogs.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed patterns and knowledge of poison frog ecology.

claim: A. femoralis and D. tinctorius occur in syntopy in the Guiana Shield.
source: A. femoralis and D. tinctorius occur in syntopy in the Guiana Shield, but A. femoralis has a wider range across Amazonia (Grant et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a taxonomic reference.

claim: A. femoralis has a wider range across Amazonia than D. tinctorius.
source: A. femoralis and D. tinctorius occur in syntopy in the Guiana Shield, but A. femoralis has a wider range across Amazonia (Grant et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a taxonomic reference.

claim: O. sylvatica is endemic to the Chocoan Rainforest of the Pacific Coast of Ecuador and Colombia.
source: O. sylvatica is endemic to the Chocoan Rainforest of the Pacific Coast of Ecuador and Colombia (Grant et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a taxonomic reference.

claim: All three poison frog species are diurnal, breed throughout the local rainy season, and shuttle tadpoles from terrestrial clutches in the leaf litter to aquatic tadpole nurseries.
source: All three species are diurnal, breed throughout the local rainy season, and shuttle tadpoles from terrestrial clutches in the leaf litter to aquatic tadpole nurseries (Grant et al., 2006; Silverstone, 1975; Silverstone, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic and natural history references.

claim: In A. femoralis, groups of up to ~20 tadpoles are predominantly transported by territorial males and deposited in terrestrial pools.
source: In A. femoralis, groups of up to ~20 tadpoles are predominantly transported by territorial males and deposited in terrestrial pools (Ringler et al., 2013; Roithmair, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In A. femoralis, females take over tadpole transport when males disappear.
source: Females take over tadpole transport when males disappear (Ringler et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In D. tinctorius, males transport one or two tadpoles at a time to terrestrial and arboreal pools.
source: In D. tinctorius, males transport one or two tadpoles at a time (but see Fischer and O'Connell, 2020; Rojas and Pašukonis, 2019 for reports of female transport) to terrestrial and arboreal pools (Fouilloux et al., 2021; Rojas, 2014; Rojas, 2015; Rojas and Pašukonis, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After tadpole deposition into pools, no further parental care is provided in A. femoralis and D. tinctorius.
source: After tadpole deposition into pools, no further parental care is provided in A. femoralis and D. tinctorius.
evidence: This is a statement about the natural history of these species based on established knowledge.

claim: In O. sylvatica, females transport one or two tadpoles at a time and deposit them into water-filled plants.
source: In contrast, in O. sylvatica, females transport one or two tadpoles at a time and deposit them into water-filled plants (Silverstone, 1973; Summers, 1992; Zimmermann and Zimmermann, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In O. sylvatica, tadpoles feed on unfertilized eggs, which the mother returns to provide every ~3–7 days.
source: Tadpoles feed on unfertilized eggs, which the mother returns to provide every ~3–7 days (this study and personal observation by E. Tapia communicated to LAC).
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and personal communication.

claim: In all three poison frog species, males and females show site fidelity, but the levels of aggressiveness and territoriality vary.
source: In all three species, males and females show site fidelity, but the levels of aggressiveness and territoriality vary.
evidence: This is a statement about the natural history of these species based on established knowledge and observations.

claim: In A. femoralis and O. sylvatica, males vocally advertise and aggressively defend small territories, while females visit males for mating and show no aggressive behavior.
source: In A. femoralis and O. sylvatica, males vocally advertise and aggressively defend small territories, while females visit males for mating and show no aggressive behavior (Fischer et al., 2020; Ringler et al., 2009; Roithmair, 1992; Silverstone, 1973; Summers, 1992; this study).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from this study.

claim: In D. tinctorius, both males and females show intrasexual aggression as part of territoriality and/or mate guarding, but males do not vocally advertise.
source: In D. tinctorius, both males and females show intrasexual aggression as part of territoriality and/or mate guarding, but males do not vocally advertise (Born et al., 2010; Rojas and Pašukonis, 2019; this study).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from this study.

claim: 311 frogs were tagged and tracked in the study.
source: We tagged and tracked 311 frogs, located each frog multiple times a day (see further below), and recorded its position and any observed behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size in the study.

claim: Five out of 311 frogs died during the study.
source: Five out of 311 frogs died during the study: one due to experimenter error, one due to an antenna snagged on the vegetation, two due to predation, and one for unknown reasons.
evidence: This is a statement about mortality in the study.

claim: Some frogs (16%) experienced skin damage ranging from superficial abrasions to deep open wounds from attachment.
source: Some frogs (16%) experienced skin damage ranging from superficial abrasions to deep open wounds from attachment.
evidence: This is a statement about tag-related injuries in the study.

claim: The prevalence of wounds varied between species (A. femoralis 6%, O. sylvatica 18%, D. tinctorius 25%).
source: The prevalence of wounds varied between species (A. femoralis 6%, O. sylvatica 18%, D. tinctorius 25%) and field seasons.
evidence: This is a statement about species differences in tag-related injuries.
